guideTitle: 5 Best Atomic Clocks with Indoor Outdoor Temperature (2026)
metaTitle: Best Atomic Clocks With Outdoor Temp (2026)
metaDescription: Five self-setting atomic clocks with wireless outdoor sensors, from jumbo 4-inch digits to a 14.5-inch wall display, compared for easy reading and setup.
mainKeyword: best atomic clocks with indoor outdoor temperature
introParagraphs: An atomic clock with an outdoor sensor tells you the time and whether to grab a coat, all from one glance. The clock sets itself from the WWVB radio signal out of Fort Collins, Colorado, and a small wireless sensor outside sends the outdoor temperature to the display. The five picks here range from the Sharp with jumbo 4-inch tall digits to the WallarGe 14.5-inch wall clock with a 12.8 by 4.9 inch LCD.

We evaluated each pick based on product specs and buyer feedback, looking at digit size, sensor range, power needs, and how clear the controls are. The La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT lists a weather-resistant sensor with a 330 foot range, the Sharp 3-inch model lists a 100 foot range, and the DAYTITOR adds 12/24-hour format and four time zones. Sensor range matters more than most buyers expect, because walls and distance cut it down.

As with any atomic clock, these keep time with quartz and only correct themselves when the radio signal arrives, mostly overnight. A window spot and fresh batteries in both the clock and the sensor matter more than the brand name, and the guide below covers that along with how to choose.

products.name: Sharp Atomic Clock with 4-Inch Display and Outdoor Sensor

specList.label: Readouts
specList.value: Time, indoor and outdoor temp, calendar, day

products.description:
The Sharp 4-inch is the easiest to read in this guide. The jumbo 4-inch tall LCD shows hours, minutes, and seconds, and it adds indoor and outdoor temperature, the calendar, and the day of the week in one view. A built-in receiver syncs with the WWVB broadcast from the US Government in Colorado, and it can hang on a wall or sit on an integrated desk stand.

The tradeoff is a second device. The outdoor sensor needs its own batteries and a placement out of direct sun and within radio range, and the listing does not give a sensor range, unlike the La Crosse.

Ownership is simple once the first sync is done. Compared with the Sharp 3-inch, it offers digits an inch bigger, and next to the La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT it trades the alarm and moon phase for a bigger readout. It is the strongest pick for anyone who wants the time visible from across the room.
products.bestFor: People who want the biggest digits plus indoor and outdoor temperature.
pros: Jumbo 4-inch digits read from across a room
Shows indoor and outdoor temperature and calendar
Works on a wall or desk stand
cons: Outdoor sensor adds another battery device

products.name: La Crosse Technology 513-1417AL-INT Atomic Clock with Outdoor Temp

specList.label: Extras
specList.value: Full calendar, HI/LO records, moon phase

products.description:
The 513-1417AL-INT is the feature leader. It monitors indoor and outdoor temperature in Fahrenheit or Celsius, tracks high and low records, and includes a weather-resistant sensor with a stated 330 foot range, the longest in the guide. The atomic time sets and readjusts automatically, with a daylight saving off option.

The tradeoffs are digit size and complexity. The 2.125-inch time digits are smaller than the Sharp 4-inch, and the extras, including a full calendar and moon phase icons, mean more settings to learn. The crescendo alarm with 10 minute snooze is helpful but is not the main reason to buy.

In ownership, the 330 foot sensor range makes placement easier than the others. It beats the Sharp 3-inch, which lists 100 feet, for homes with a detached garage or a long yard, while the Sharp wins on digit size.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want long sensor range plus alarm, calendar, and high and low records.
pros: Tracks high and low temperature records
Auto sets and readjusts for daylight saving
cons: More settings and icons to learn

products.name: Sharp Atomic Digital Wall Clock with 3-Inch Display and Outdoor Sensor

specList.label: Readouts
specList.value: Indoor and outdoor temp, calendar, weekday

products.description:
The Sharp 3-inch is a balanced pick. It uses large high-contrast numbers that are described as readable from bed, a sofa, or across an office, and it syncs automatically with the US atomic clock with automatic daylight saving. The included wireless sensor shows real-time outdoor temperature next to the indoor reading.

The sensor range is its main limit. A 100 foot range is the shortest stated in this guide, so thick walls or a far-off placement may cut reception. The digits are also smaller than the 4-inch sibling.

In use it is an easy, no-fuss clock. Next to the Sharp 4-inch it gives up an inch of digit height, and against the La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT it has a shorter sensor range but a simpler layout.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and offices that want a simple jumbo display with outdoor temperature nearby.
cons: 100 ft sensor range is the shortest here

products.name: WallarGe 14.5-Inch Atomic Clock with Indoor Outdoor Temperature

specList.label: Readouts
specList.value: Time, date, day, indoor and outdoor temp

products.description:
This WallarGe is built for walls and big rooms. The LCD is 12.8 by 4.9 inches, which makes it the largest overall screen in the guide, and it displays temperature, date, day, and time together. A built-in receiver syncs with the WWVB broadcast so it never needs setting.

The indoor reading comes from a built-in sensor, while the outdoor reading depends on a wireless sensor that needs its own placement. A screen this big suits kitchens, dens, and workshops more than a small bedroom. The listing does not state sensor range, so verify placement before mounting.

Ownership is simple after the first sync. Against the Sharp 4-inch it offers a much larger overall display but smaller individual digits, and compared with the DAYTITOR it is bigger but carries fewer listed settings.
products.bestFor: Big walls where the whole display should be readable from across a large room.
pros: Shows time, date, day, and both temperatures

products.name: DAYTITOR 10.5-Inch Atomic Wall Clock with Indoor Outdoor Temp
products.description:
The DAYTITOR adds control that others skip. A 10.5-inch LCD shows the time, and the settings let you pick 12 or 24-hour format and one of four time zones. A high-precision indoor sensor and an outdoor reading give both temperatures, and WWVB data updates the clock automatically.

The flip side is that more options mean more to learn, and the listing gives no outdoor sensor range. It is mid-sized, so it will not read from as far away as the WallarGe 14.5-inch.

It works well for a kitchen or office where someone wants to choose the format. Next to the Sharp 3-inch it offers more settings but less documentation on range, and it is the pick if 24-hour format matters.
products.bestFor: Owners who want to choose 12 or 24-hour format and their time zone.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Readability decides how useful the clock is. The Sharp 4-inch has jumbo 4-inch digits, the Sharp 3-inch has 3-inch numbers, and the La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT has 2.125-inch digits. Pick the largest digits that fit, and favor high-contrast numerals, since the whole point is a quick glance.

The La Crosse states a 330 ft sensor range and the Sharp 3-inch states 100 ft, while the others give no range. Walls, metal siding, and distance cut range in real homes, so choose a long stated range if the sensor will be far away. Place the sensor on a shaded north-facing wall to avoid sun heating.
Two devices mean two sets of batteries, and low batteries are a common reason atomic clocks stop syncing. Use fresh alkaline batteries in both, and replace them on a fixed date once a year.

All five depend on the 60 kHz WWVB signal from Fort Collins, which reaches about 2,000 miles. Reception is best overnight, and NIST advises keeping the clock 1 to 2 meters from monitors and placing it near a window facing Colorado. Rotate a desktop unit 90 degrees if the sync fails.

The La Crosse adds alarm, high and low records, and moon phase, while the DAYTITOR adds format and time zone choices. Each extra is another thing to learn. Choose only the features you will check daily.

The Sharp 4-inch can hang or sit on an integrated stand, while the WallarGe 14.5-inch is built for a wall. Decide where the clock will live before buying, since a desk stand matters for shelves and counters.

The Sharp 4-inch led with 4-inch digits, and the WallarGe 14.5-inch led for overall screen size, while the La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT has the smallest digits at 2.125 inches. howWeEvaluated.title: Sensor performance claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at stated sensor range and construction. The La Crosse led with a weather-resistant sensor at 330 ft, and the Sharp 3-inch lists 100 ft. Models with no stated range scored lower on documentation.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup effort
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted steps from unboxing to a working clock and sensor. The Sharp models are the simplest, while the DAYTITOR asks for format and zone choices. Fewer steps scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery burden
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered that every pick has two devices to power. We favored clear battery information and easy access, and we noted that models with extras use more power. The most basic pick, the Sharp 3-inch, scored best for simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Features that matter
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed alarm, records, moon phase, and format choices against complexity. The La Crosse earned credit for records and alarm, and the DAYTITOR for control. Extras only counted if they help daily use.

faq.q: How do I choose between a Sharp and La Crosse atomic clock with outdoor sensor?
faq.a: Choose the Sharp 4-inch for the biggest digits and the simplest layout. Choose the La Crosse 513-1417AL-INT for the 330 ft sensor range, alarm, and high and low records. Both set themselves from the atomic signal.

faq.q: Are these clocks costly to run?
faq.a: Running costs are low, since they use standard batteries in the clock and the sensor. Fresh alkaline cells replaced yearly keep syncing reliable.

faq.q: How do I maintain the outdoor sensor?
faq.a: Keep it out of direct sun and rain beyond its rating, replace its batteries on schedule, and wipe it with a dry cloth.
It can be, if the sensor is shaded. Sun on the sensor inflates the reading, so mount it on a shaded wall away from heat sources like dryer vents.

faq.q: Why does my sensor lose connection?
faq.a: Common causes are weak batteries, distance, and walls. The La Crosse states 330 ft and the Sharp 3-inch states 100 ft, and real range is shorter through walls. Move the sensor closer or replace batteries.

faq.q: Do these clocks work everywhere in the United States?
faq.a: Manufacturers cite roughly 2,000 miles from Fort Collins, but reception is not guaranteed. Metal and concrete can block it, so test overnight near a window.

faq.q: Why is my clock not setting itself?
faq.a: Check batteries, move it near a window facing Colorado, keep it 1 to 2 meters from monitors, and leave it overnight. Rotate it 90 degrees if needed.
